PREEMPTIVE FIX applied to every remaining child (orchestrator, 2026-09-03 19:15). The ancora-v1n verification exposed a defect in how I wrote these tickets, and rather than let it bounce ticket after ticket I audited all fourteen and fixed it in one pass.

The defect: a ticket's Allowed touches permitted a production file while withholding the subject spec that governs it. Under ancora's own rules, editing that file raises drift that ONLY a substantive edit to that spec can clear, so the worker is left choosing between a mechanical scope violation and shipping a corpus that contradicts itself. ancora-v1n chose silently, retagging two tests onto a new requirement and inverting them, which left a clause in ancora.gate.two_append_guards both untrue and covered by no test, while the gate stayed quiet because that requirement kept five other tagged tests.

Method, so this is checkable rather than asserted: I parsed the Modules line at the head of each of the seven subject specs, derived the lib path for every module, and cross-checked each ticket's Allowed lib files against the specs it lists. Seven of eleven not-yet-started children had at least one gap.

- ancora-gqb: permits lib/ancora/derive files, missing ancora.derive
- ancora-n24: permits lib/ancora/append_only.ex, missing ancora.gate
- ancora-11w: permits lib/ancora/git.ex and lib/ancora/trailer.ex, missing ancora.derive and ancora.findings
- ancora-sfu: missing ancora.derive, ancora.findings, ancora.tasks
- ancora-xla.1: eleven lib files, missing ancora.derive, ancora.gate, ancora.review, ancora.tasks
- ancora-xla.6: nineteen lib files, missing ancora.derive, ancora.findings, ancora.parsing
- ancora-xla.8: missing ancora.derive

Each addition names the specific permitted file that triggers it, and is constrained to acknowledgment edits for that ticket's own changes, never weakening a must and never deleting a requirement. This is not blanket permission to rewrite other subjects.

Separately, every one of the fourteen children now carries this clause, including the three in flight: any spec whose stated rule the ticket's change makes false may be corrected in the same diff, and doing so is expected rather than tolerated. That is the rule ancora-v1n needed and did not have. A worker that finds it has falsified a requirement should now fix it and say so, instead of routing around it.

Four children needed no spec additions and already listed what they touch: ancora-xla.3, ancora-xla.5, ancora-xla.7, ancora-xla.9.

Honest note on cost: this is seven bounces that would probably have happened one at a time, each burning an implementation attempt and a grader pair. It is also seven chances to ship a self-contradicting corpus from a project whose entire product is a spec gate. Finding it took one cold verification that I did not want to hear.

GRADING LADDER RESULTS, first three tickets (orchestrator, 2026-09-03 19:25). Both cold verifications failed, both catches are real, and neither was visible to any automated check in this repository.

ancora-v1n: VERIFY FAIL, then AUDIT BOUNCE to implementer. The audit did not inherit the verifier's finding; it re-derived the counts, confirmed all three gaps, and found the verifier UNDER-read one of them. Not only did the 'or its subject id' clause lose its test, all four authorization tests moved to the parsing tag, so the entire suppression half of ancora.gate.two_append_guards now has zero tests under its own id while five other tagged tests keep spec/requirement_unverified silent. Remedy is three specified edits: delete the false clause from the requirement statement, correct the contradicted scenario's given, and dual-tag two tests using the list form the tag scanner already supports. Respawned as attempt 2 of 2 with the audit comment verbatim; the widened Allowed touches mean the remedy is now legal, which it was not on attempt 1. Bounce count 1.

ancora-xla.2: VERIFY FAIL, now in audit. Two gaps. The serious one is a REGRESSION in a ticket whose entire purpose is eliminating verdict-less crashes: an unreadable test file used to produce a clean tags/parse_error finding and a proper tier=branch verdict, and now produces empty stdout and a RuntimeError on stderr. The verifier traced the mechanism precisely, that a with's else never sees its own body's return value, so gate_error/1 is unreachable from the four converted sites, and reproduced it against a scratch fixture at both trees. The spec clause promising env-tier handling of unreadable inputs is therefore written but not implemented.

The second gap is the one I asked it to check specifically, and it paid off. The implementer claimed a close path went from 500.7 ms to 14.7 ms. The verifier re-measured 20 samples per scenario across two named trees and found the opposite: base 0.02 to 0.08 ms against head 10.58 to 10.77 ms. Every head sample sits just above the 10 ms bound, because Port.close/1 terminates synchronously and never delivers an exit status, so the wait the new spec clause describes can never succeed. The call got roughly 300x slower and the clause is vacuous. That is exactly the vacuous-comparison failure mode the ship session's auditor caught this morning, caught again, this time before it merged.

Grader tally so far: 3 cold verifications, 2 audits, 1 bounce, 0 escalations. Two of three verified tickets came back FAIL, and in both cases the implementation was substantially correct with a specific hole. That ratio is the ladder working, not workers underperforming.

- [untested-clause] Moving a @tag from one requirement to another can silently orphan everything the old requirement proved. spec/requirement_unverified stays quiet as long as any other tagged test remains. (from ancora-v1n)
- [other] A green gate proves neither a consistent corpus nor a true spec clause. Two tickets have now added spec sentences describing behaviour the code does not implement, and the gate passed both. Write the clause to match what you built. (from ancora-v1n, ancora-xla.2)

ADMISSION DEFECT, third instance, and the sweep that closes it (orchestrator, 2026-09-03 19:40).

The ancora-xla.4 verifier found the same class of defect a third time, in a new flavour, and this one is structurally guaranteed rather than merely likely. Ancora.PolicyFiles.missing_decision?/1 at lib/ancora/policy_files.ex:115 fires change/missing_decision whenever any path under .spec/specs/ changes without an accompanying decision-record change in the SAME diff. Every child of this epic is required to edit a spec. Eight of fourteen permitted that edit while withholding .spec/decisions/**, so every one of them would have hit a forced finding with no legal way to clear it: ancora-11w, ancora-xla.1, ancora-xla.3, ancora-xla.4, ancora-xla.5, ancora-xla.6, ancora-xla.7, ancora-xla.8. ancora-kzw, P0, labelled security, filed standalone: a hostile git tree escapes the base-view write root. Ancora.BaseView.materialize writes every blob using the path git reports verbatim. A tree entry can be literally named '..'. git mktree accepts it, ls-tree -r emits the joined path, git resolves it on read, Path.join leaves it in place, and the kernel resolves it at File.write! so the file lands outside the temp root at attacker-chosen depth. The escaped file also survives the File.rm_rf cleanup at gate.ex:67 and review.ex:41, because it was never inside the root.

This matters because ancora is a gate that runs against repositories its operator does not control.

I was WRONG about this and the record should show it. When the ancora-xla.8 verifier reported it, I tried to reproduce, could not, and wrote a note saying so: git refused the path shape that would escape, and the shape it accepted joined back to a directory where the write fails. I explicitly declined to report a vulnerability to Manuel on evidence I could not confirm, and routed it to audit naming the three-level shape as the candidate I had not built. That was the right process and the wrong conclusion.

The auditor built exactly that shape and it works. Nest 'a' then '..' then '..' around a blob, and ls-tree emits 'a/../../evil.txt'. I then reproduced it a third time myself before filing: git returns the blob for that path with exit 0, and the join expands one directory above the root. The mechanism explains both of my earlier observations and is worth recording because it will mislead the next reader too: git normalises a rev:path string ONLY when the path starts with './' or '../', which is what produces 'outside repository'. Anything else is a literal component walk against tree entry NAMES, so an embedded '..' matches an entry named '..'. A two-level probe therefore finds nothing and looks conclusive.

Confirmed from both sides: '<rev>:../evil.txt' is refused; '<rev>:a/./../../evil.txt' fails for want of an entry named '.'; '<rev>:a/../../evil.txt' succeeds. The auditor also confirmed both read paths are affected, batch port and fallback alike.

Three agents reproduced it independently before it was written down as fact. That is the standard this epic has been holding and it is why the report is trustworthy.
